summary: Every noun is masculine or feminine, and most nouns add -s or -es in the plural.
Adjectives change to match the noun and usually come after it, as in una casa blanca.
Compare people and things with más, menos and tan, and say which is the most with el más.
Choose between el, la, un and una, and learn when Spanish leaves the article out.
Point to things with este, ese and aquel, depending on how far away they are.
Say whose something is with mi, tu and su before the noun, or with mío and tuyo after it.
Talk about amounts with mucho, poco, bastante, demasiado and todo, and know when to say muy.
Use algo, alguien and alguno, their opposites nada, nadie and ninguno, and the double negative in no veo nada.
Learn when to say or leave out yo, tú and the other subject words, and when to use usted.
Replace the object of a verb with lo, la, le and their plurals, combine them as se lo, and learn when Spain uses le for a man.
Say what you like with me gusta and me gustan, and use encantar, interesar, doler and parecer the same way.
Use me, te, se, nos and os with verbs like llamarse and levantarse, for actions you do to yourself.
After words like para and de, use mí and ti instead of yo and tú, and with con say conmigo and contigo.
Add details about a thing or a place with que and donde, as in el libro que leo and la calle donde vivo.
Ask questions with qué, quién, cómo, dónde, cuándo, cuánto and cuál, and learn when to use qué or cuál.
In positive commands the pronouns join the end of the verb, as in dímelo and siéntate.

title_es: Ir a, tener que y hay que
summary: Talk about plans with ir a and about what you must do with tener que and hay que.

title_es: Acabar de, volver a y empezar a
title_en: Have just, do again, start to
summary: Say you have just done something with acabar de, do it again with volver a, and start it with empezar a.
Use estar and the gerund for what is happening right now, as in estoy comiendo.
Use ser for what something is, estar for where it is or how it is, and hay to say that it exists.
Put a before a person who is the object of the verb, as in veo a María, but not before a thing.
Use a for movement and clock times, en for where something is, and de for origin and owner.
Use para for goals, destinations and deadlines, and por for causes, routes, exchanges and rough times.
Say how long ago something happened with hace, and since when or for how long with desde and desde hace.
Give a reason with porque after the main idea, or with como at the start of the sentence.
Talk about real possibilities with si and the present, as in si llueve, me quedo en casa.
Turn an adjective into a noun with lo, as in lo mejor (the best part), and use lo que for what, as in lo que quiero (what I want).
Use se for what people do in general or for what is done, as in se habla español and se venden pisos.
Describe accidents with se and a pronoun, as in se me olvidó and se le cayó, so the action sounds unplanned.

title_es: Quien, el que y la que
title_en: Describing with quien and el que
summary: Use quien for people and el que or la que after a preposition, as in la casa en la que vivo.
Say maybe with a lo mejor and the indicative, or with quizás and tal vez, which can take the subjunctive.

title_es: Además, sin embargo y así que
summary: Link your ideas with además to add, sin embargo to contrast, and así que or por eso to give a result.
In negative commands the pronouns go before the verb, as in no me lo digas and no te preocupes.

title_es: Dejar de, ponerse a y estar a punto de
summary: Say you stop doing something with dejar de, start suddenly with ponerse a, and are about to with estar a punto de.
Say how long something has gone on with llevar, as in llevo un año estudiando, and that it still goes on with seguir.
Some adjectives change their meaning with ser or estar, as in ser listo (clever) and estar listo (ready).
Some verbs always take the same preposition, such as pensar en, soñar con, depender de and acordarse de.
Express hopes and good wishes with ojalá or que and the subjunctive, as in ojalá llueva and que te vaya bien.
When you want, ask or advise someone else to do something, use que and the subjunctive, as in quiero que vengas.
After phrases like es importante que or me alegra que, the next verb goes in the subjunctive.

title_es: Creo que y no creo que
summary: Creo que takes the indicative, but no creo que and dudo que take the subjunctive.
Pass on what someone says or said with dice que and dijo que, and change the verb where needed.
Use the subjunctive after que when you describe something you are looking for or that may not exist.
After cuando and hasta que, use the subjunctive when you talk about the future, as in cuando llegues, llámame.
Use para and the infinitive when the subject stays the same, and para que and the subjunctive when it changes.
Add a contrast with aunque or a pesar de when you state a fact, as in aunque llueve, salgo.
In careful writing, use el cual after prepositions and cuyo to say whose, as in el autor cuyo libro leí.
Use ser and a participle to focus on what was done, mostly in news and formal writing, as in fue construido en 1900.
When the main verb is in the past or the conditional, the subjunctive verb is in the past too, as in quería que vinieras.
When you report past words, vendré becomes vendría and he venido becomes había venido.
Compare with an imagined situation using como si and the past subjunctive, as in habla como si lo supiera todo.
Imagine unlikely or unreal situations with si and the past subjunctive, as in si tuviera tiempo, viajaría.
Talk about how the past could have been different, as in si lo hubiera sabido, habría venido.
Set conditions without si, using en caso de que, con tal de que or a no ser que and the subjunctive.

title_es: Más de lo que, cuanto más
summary: Compare whole ideas with más de lo que and cuanto más, as in cuanto más leo, más entiendo.
Use aunque with the subjunctive when the fact is unknown or does not matter, as in aunque llueva, iré.
